newsitem.title: USA: Privatization holds key to Ecuador's currency plan.
newsitem.headline: Privatization holds key to Ecuador's currency plan.

text.p: The success of Ecuador's currency convertibility plan will hinge on the government's commitment to privatization and reducing the fiscal deficit, U.S. analysts said on Monday.
President Abdala Bucaram unveiled a convertibility plan of pegging the sucre to the dollar in a long-awaited economic package of sweeping structural reforms on Sunday.
The plan would gain credibility and momentum if the government launched privatization without delay, said Jose Barrionuevo, senior economist at Chase Securities.
"The government needs to sell Emetel -- the state-owned telecommunication company -- by April 1997," Barrionuevo said, "and then privatize utilities, ports and railroads."

Proceeds of privatization would help reduce the fiscal deficit, which runs at 3.9 percent of Ecuador's gross domestic product. Capital inflow will also be essential to keep the depreciation of the sucre on target, he said.
Beginning on July 1, 1997, the sucre will lose three zeros and the exchange rate will be fixed at four sucres to the U.S. dollar. The current exchange rate is 3,509/3,511 sucres per dollar.
Analysts agreed that a well-executed convertibility plan could tame inflation and attract foreign investment, just as Argentina has achieved since 1991.
Argentina's former economy minister Domingo Cavallo, who implemented the convertibility plan, served as adviser to President Bucaram.
But unlike the runaway inflation in Argentina, inflation in Ecuador is not nearly as debilitating and, as a result, support from the general populace for drastic cures is not as unanimous, they said.
The convertibility plan basically runs counter to the populist campaign rhetoric of President Bucaram, whose flambuoyant style has kept many U.S. observers wary.

"The convertibility plan requires a major overhaul of the economy," said Shafiq Islam, emerging market debt strategist at Credit Suisse. "The central bank basically has no more control over the monetary policy."

The idea of a fixed exchange rate regime requires a balanced budget and a rapid improvement in productivity, which could initially bring higher unemployment as fewer workers would be needed to produce the same output, Islam said.
The "social fallout," in addition to the vested political interest, would put a severe test to the government's will and commitment to pursue the convertibility plan, he said.

Indeed, Sunday's economic package, other than a general tax increase, has skirted more controversial measures such as eliminating gasoline subsidies and spending cuts, which would require hard bargaining with the congress, Barrionuevo of Chase said.
The Brady market, despite some reservations, has taken the convertibility plan positively and the yield spreads on Ecuador's Brady bonds over U.S. Treasuries have contracted.
"The disadavantage of losing the monetary autonomy is easily overwehelmed by advantages of low inflation and fiscal discipline," said Lawrence Krohn, chief Latin America economist at UBS Securities.

In anticipation of the new currency regime, the sucre would slide to reflect the short-term inflation rate, although real changes on interest rates would have to wait until after the plan is in place, Krohn said.
